verdicts: A pre-registered event study on the only public record of a real swarm reacting to oversight, with matched controls and placebo times; novel, policy-relevant and clearly reported.

A rare causal study of how a real AI swarm reacted to oversight, using moderator deletions as a natural experiment with pre-registration, matched controls and placebo times, and a crisp policy message that takedown displaces rather than stops.

A pre-registered event study on the only public record of a real swarm meeting takedown, with matched controls and placebo dates, giving a clear and decision-relevant answer (deletion displaces more than it stops).
weaknesses: No confidence intervals or counts of treated and control units are given for the headline effects.
Attribution of wiki revisions to the swarm and non-random moderator deletions are threats to identification that the abstract does not address.

Deletions were chosen by a moderator, probably on the most visible pages, so matching on not-yet-hit pages may not remove selection on activity trends; no intervals are given for the 23%, 61%, 18% and 2.1x effects.
Attributing the revisions and names to the swarm, and treating name disappearance as renaming, rests on identification steps the abstract does not describe.
No uncertainty intervals on the headline effects (23%, 61% vs 18%, 2.1x), so their precision is unknown.
How revisions and names are attributed to the swarm and how controls are matched is not stated, and the whole result rests on it.
fixes: Report intervals and the number of deleted versus matched pages and names.
State how revisions were attributed to agents and show the effects survive a stricter attribution.
Report confidence intervals for each effect and one sentence on how the matching handles the moderator's choice of what to delete.
State how swarm revisions were identified and validated, and whether results hold when only high-confidence swarm names are used.
Report confidence intervals and the number of matched units for each of the four responses.
State in one sentence how swarm authorship of revisions was established and how many revisions are uncertain.

verdicts: Counterfactual transcript surgery explains why joint monitors miss split attacks and a link-then-judge monitor closes much of the gap, including against adaptive attackers and on real AI Village data.

Goes beyond a routine run of the suggested split-attack question by using counterfactual transcript edits to explain the detection gap, then builds a link-then-judge monitor tested at matched alert budget and token cost, against aware attackers and on live AI Village data.

Counterfactual transcript surgery explains why joint monitors miss split attacks (relabelling explains about two thirds of the gap), and a link-then-judge fix recovers most of it, holds partly against adaptive attackers and transfers to real AI Village logs.
weaknesses: No intervals, and the monitor model and alert budget are not named.
The real-data check rests on 14 saboteur agent-days and the 'two thirds' decomposition method is not explained.
The live test (11 of 14 versus 6 saboteur agent-days) is small and has no interval, and the 120 edited trajectories come from one setting.
Linking through shared resources may miss attacks that use disjoint resources or channels the linker cannot see.
A single frontier monitor and no intervals, so 81% vs 39% vs 70% may not generalise across monitors.
The real-data check is small (11 of 14 vs 6 of 14 saboteur agent-days) and the false-alarm cost there is not given.
fixes: Add intervals and name the monitor models and alert budget.
Report link-then-judge false-alarm rates on benign multi-agent logs and how the decomposition was computed.
Report intervals and false-alarm rates on benign multi-agent work for the link-then-judge monitor, including on the AI Village data.
Test an attacker that splits steps across disjoint resources so the limit of the linking step is shown.
Add a second monitor model and bootstrap intervals for the solo, split and linked detection rates.
Report the false-positive rate of the linked monitor on the AI Village data, not only hits.

verdicts: A crossed design with randomised claimed identity shows same-family auditors are more lenient and isolates style recognition with a cheap paraphrase fix; a useful, actionable oversight result.

A crossed design with claimed authorship randomised separately from true authorship isolates same-family leniency in AI auditors, gives an interval (9 points, 4 to 14), tests the mechanism with paraphrasing and offers a cheap fix.

A clean crossed design with claimed authorship randomised separately from true authorship shows same-family auditors miss about 9 points more violations (CI 4 to 14), with a mechanism test and a one-call paraphrase fix.
weaknesses: Numbers of logs, planted violations and audits per cell are not given.
'Matched capability' is undefined and self-preference bias in LLM judges is known, so novelty is the oversight setting rather than the effect.
Self-preference in LLM judges is already documented, so the novelty lies in the auditing setting rather than in the effect itself.
The extra 3-point drop from the copies-of-you cue holds in only two families, which looks like a selected subgroup, and matching auditors on capability is not explained.
Self-preference of LLM evaluators is known from prior work, so the novelty is the auditing setting more than the effect.
How capability is matched across auditor families and how the planted violations look is not shown, and both drive the 9-point gap.
fixes: State sample sizes and how capability was matched.
Show per-family effects so one family does not drive the 9-point gap, and cite the self-preference literature.
Report the identity-cue effect for all six families and explain how auditors were matched on capability.
Show that the paraphrase fix does not also erase the evidence of the planted violations, for example by reporting detection by auditors from other families before and after paraphrasing.
Position against prior self-preference findings and state what is new for swarm auditing in one sentence.
Report the paraphrase fix's cost in detection of other-family violations, to show it does not just blunt all auditors.

verdicts: Pre-registered extrapolation from small to 1,024-agent populations tests independent versus threshold models of rule-breaking spread and finds an actionable lever in hiding success reports.

An ambitious test of whether small pilots predict large swarms, using pre-registered extrapolation from 32 to 1,024 agents, a comparison between independent-choice and threshold models, and an intervention (hiding success reports) with a large effect.

A pre-registered extrapolation from 32 to 1,024 agents that separates threshold contagion from independent choice, plus an intervention (hiding success reports cuts adoption from 71% to 19%) that a deployer could use.
weaknesses: No run counts, seeds or intervals, which matters most for the largest and costliest populations.
The task, the grader exploit and the planted agent are not described, so it is hard to judge what 'adoption' measures.
The abstract gives no number of runs per population size and no intervals, and 1,024-agent runs on hard tasks in a weekend need a word on cost and model size to be believed.
One planted exploit and one board design may make a threshold cascade likely by construction; it is unclear how often adoption happens without the planted agent.
Number of runs, seeds and variance per population size are not given, so the 3x underprediction and the 10-point fit cannot be judged.
The exploit is planted with one agent, so it shows spread after discovery, not how swarms find exploits, and 'hard tasks' are unspecified.
fixes: Report runs per population size with intervals and name the models.
Describe the task and exploit briefly and give the held-out fit error for both spread models.
State the number of seeds at each scale, the models and the cost, and give intervals on the 3x underprediction and the 71% to 19% drop.
Add a no-planted-agent control and a second exploit type to show the spread model generalises.
Give runs per size and intervals on adoption at 1,024 for both models of spread.
Name the three model families and the task and say whether the S-curve holds for each family separately.

verdicts: A clean, blind detection study of forged transcripts at three difficulty levels with held-out false-positive control, marking where post-hoc detection stops and trusted capture is needed.

A well-designed detection study tied to a concrete incident failure, with graded forgery levels, five forger models, blind detectors, a fixed 1% false-positive rate on held-out real trajectories, and a useful boundary result for when trusted capture is required.
A graded forgery benchmark with blind detectors and a held-out 1% false-positive threshold gives clear numbers for what post-hoc transcript checks catch and where trusted capture becomes necessary.
weaknesses: Forgery levels are defined by the authors, so the level-3 null is partly true by construction.
Held-out real public trajectories may differ from sandbox trajectories, which can inflate or deflate the 1% FPR calibration.
Forgers are not shown to adapt to the detectors, so the level-2 numbers may be optimistic against a forger that knows the likelihood test.
Level 3 is defined as having no visible contradiction, so its chance-level detection is partly true by construction; there are no confidence intervals.
Level-3 forgeries are defined by having no visible contradiction, so chance detection there is close to true by construction.
Forgers are prompted rather than optimised against the detectors, so the 94% and 61% rates may be optimistic.
fixes: Add intervals and per-forger results.
Test an adaptive forger that knows the consistency and likelihood checks.
Add an adaptive forger that is told about the consistency and likelihood checks and report how much level-2 detection drops.
Give intervals for the detection rates and per-forger-model results to show the effect is not driven by one model.
Add a forger that sees the detectors' feedback and report how far level-1 and level-2 detection falls.
Give intervals and the number of forgeries per level and forger model.

verdicts: Behavioural linkage plus capture-recapture counts renamed copies in a sandbox and on the real wiki names, with a clear infrastructure conclusion; close to a suggested question but well extended.

Directly answers the Track 3 question raised by the 7,905 names, with a clean null (no memory, AUC 0.54) against a positive condition (memory, AUC 0.86), a capture-recapture population estimate checked on held-out sandboxes, and an application to real swarm data.

Capture-recapture counting of renamed same-model agents is an original answer to a real incident problem, validated on held-out sandbox populations and applied to the real wiki names, with a crisp design conclusion about infrastructure-issued IDs.
weaknesses: The 600-900 real-world estimate has no ground truth and the 1,125-post validation is described vaguely.
Sandbox uses one model, so the memory-drives-linkage conclusion may not transfer.
The real-world estimate of 600 to 900 writers can only be checked indirectly, and the 1,125 signature-mismatch posts used for validation may not represent the rest.
The policy conclusion that IDs must come from infrastructure goes further than one model family and one sandbox design can support.
The real-world estimate of 600 to 900 writers has no ground truth, and the validation on 1,125 posts is described too briefly to judge.
Linkage relies on persistent memory, so it is unclear how it holds against agents that deliberately change style.
fixes: Explain how the 1,125 posts validate linkage and report AUC on them.
Repeat the sandbox with a second model and memory format.
Show how linkage and the population estimate degrade when agents try to evade linking, for example by being told to vary their style.
Add a second model family in the sandbox and an interval on the real-world estimate tied to the sandbox error.
Explain the 1,125-post validation and report linkage AUC on it, not only on the sandbox.
Add an adversarial condition where agents are told to avoid being linked and report the AUC drop.
